summary: Gathers use cases and requirements for provisioning data that helps SIP service providers route sessions, focusing on a "registry" element. DRINKS stands for Data for Reachability of Inter-/Intra-NetworK SIP. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a call can be routed, the network that receives it has to know where to send it. That information is called session establishment data. This RFC collects the situations that arise when providers share that data through a central registry, and turns them into a list of requirements a future protocol has to meet.

questions: how do sip providers exchange routing data
what is a registry in sip routing
subtitle: The situations that arise when telephone and SIP providers share routing data, and the requirements a protocol for it must meet.

tldr.problem: Session establishment data tells a provider where to send a call, but RFC 5486 says nothing about how that data is provisioned between providers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC collects the use cases for sharing session establishment data through a registry and turns them into 26 numbered requirements in seven groups, covering provisioning, peering, exchange models, record content, grouping, identifier handling and portability.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document, not a protocol. Its purpose is to let the designers of a future provisioning protocol say which of the requirements they meet.

today: RFC 6461 is an Informational document, and the metadata shows no obsoleting and no updating RFC. It sets out the requirements a DRINKS provisioning protocol would have to meet, so it is a requirements document rather than a specification of such a protocol.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
RFC 5486 defines Session Establishment Data, or SED, as the data used to route a call to the next hop associated with the called domain's ingress point, and more specifically as the set of parameters that the outgoing signaling path border elements (SBEs) need to establish a session. RFC 5486 does not specify the protocol or format for provisioning SED. To pave the way for specifying such a protocol, this document presents the use cases and associated requirements that have been proposed to provision SED.

SED is typically created by the terminating or next-hop SIP service provider (SSP) and consumed by the originating SSP. To avoid a multitude of bilateral exchanges, SED is often shared via intermediary systems, termed registries within this document. Such registries receive data via provisioning transactions from SSPs, and then distribute the received data into Local Data Repositories (LDRs), which are used for call routing by outgoing SBEs.

This document addresses the use cases and requirements for provisioning registries. Data distribution to local data repositories is out of scope. The resulting provisioning protocol can be used to provision data into a registry, or between multiple registries operating in parallel.

The RFC also proposes two aggregation groups: aggregation of public identifiers into a destination group, and aggregation of SED records into a route group.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a call can be routed, the network that receives it has to know where to send it. That information is called session establishment data. This RFC collects the situations that arise when providers share that data through a central registry, and turns them into a list of requirements a future protocol has to meet.

sections.title: Terminology and the Data Model
sections.content:
The document reuses terms from RFC 3261 such as SIP, from RFC 5486 such as SSP, LUF, LRF and SED, and from RFC 5067 such as carrier-of-record and transit provider, and adds the following. A registry is the authoritative source for provisioned session establishment data and related information; it can be part of an SSP or an independent entity. A registrar is an entity that provisions and manages data into the registry; an SSP can act as its own registrar or delegate the function to a third party who acts as its registrar. A Local Data Repository (LDR) is the data store component of an addressing server that provides resolution responses. A public identifier refers to a telephone number, a SIP address, or other identity as deemed appropriate, such as a globally routable URI of a user address. A telephone number (TN) range is a numerically contiguous set of telephone numbers, and a TN prefix is a preceding portion of the digits common across a series of E.164 numbers, including all the valid E.164 numbers that satisfy the expansion rules mandated by the country or region with which they comply. A routing number (RN) is a routing number as described in RFC 4694.

Two aggregations tie the data together. A destination group is an aggregation of a set of public identifiers, TN ranges or RNs that share common SED, which is exposed to a common set of peers. A route group is an aggregation that contains a related set of SED records and is associated with a set of destination groups, which facilitates the management of SED records for one or more data recipients. A data recipient is an entity with visibility into a specific set of public identifiers, or TN ranges or RNs, the destination groups that contain them, and a route group's SED records.

The data model relates these objects in fixed ways. A public identifier can be directly related to zero or more SED records, and an SED record relates to exactly one public identifier. A destination group can contain zero or more TN ranges, zero or more public identifiers and zero or more RNs, and each of those is contained in exactly one destination group. A route group can contain zero or more SED records, each contained in exactly one route group, and a route group can be associated with zero or more destination groups, which in turn can be associated with zero or more route groups. A data recipient can be associated with zero or more route groups, and a route group can refer to zero or more data recipients.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC defines the objects it needs: the registry that holds the data, the registrar that writes into it, the local copy each provider routes calls from, and two levels of grouping. A destination group collects the numbers and addresses that share the same route; a route group collects the routing data itself and links it to those groups.

sections.title: Registry Use Cases
sections.content:
Section 3 documents seven categories of use case for provisioning the registry. Any request to provision, modify or delete data is subject to security considerations, and the protocols that implement these use cases will need to identify and address them explicitly.

Provisioning mechanisms. Real-time provisioning is the case where registrars have operational systems that provision public identifiers, or TN ranges or RNs in association with their SED, and that expect or require the activity to be completed immediately, as opposed to an out-of-band or batch scheme at a later time. Non-real-time bulk provisioning is the opposite: requests are batched up into large sets and processed out of band at a later time. Multi-request provisioning covers the case where an SSP performs several provisioning actions on several objects in a single request or transaction, done for performance and scalability and for transactional reasons, so that the set of actions either fails or succeeds atomically as a complete set.

Interconnect schemes. Inter-SSP SED covers SSPs creating peering relationships with other SSPs in order to establish interconnects, which involves communicating and enabling the points of ingress and other SED used to establish sessions. Direct and indirect peering distinguishes peering set up for public identifiers where the SSP is the carrier-of-record from peering set up for identifiers where the SSP is a transit provider. Intra-SSP SED covers the establishment of sessions between an SSP's own public identifiers, where intra-SSP signaling points and other SED can differ from the inter-SSP ones. Selective peering covers the case where peering relationships often result in different points of ingress or other SED for the same set of public identifiers, done on a route group basis. Provisioning of a delegated hierarchy covers an SSP that maintains its own infrastructure containing the route records that constitute the terminal step in the LUF, and provisions registries to direct queries for its public identifiers to that infrastructure rather than provisioning the route records directly; for DNS-based route records such a delegated hierarchy makes use of NS and CNAME records, while a flat structure makes use of NAPTR resource records.

SED exchange and discovery models. Three models are described. One exchanges or receives SED that is the aggregated result of both LUF and LRF. One exchanges only LUF data, using domain names, which the peer then resolves independently via RFC 3263 to the final points of ingress data and other SED. One exchanges only an administrative domain identifier, which is not necessarily resolvable via DNS, after which the process of using that identifier to select points of ingress can be SSP specific and is out of scope. Some SSPs need to support all three concurrently for the same set of public identifiers.

SED record content, data management and identifiers. Establishing interconnects involves communicating points of ingress, the service types such as SIP and SIPS supported by each point of ingress, and the relative priority of each point of ingress for each service type. Querying SSPs sometimes cache SED that was looked up earlier, so a time-to-live may be associated with a given SED record. On data management, an SSP's operational practices often separate the responsibility for provisioning points of ingress and other SED from the responsibility for provisioning public identifiers, so that a network engineer can establish a physical interconnect with a peering SSP's network and provision the associated domain name, host and IP addressing information, while the provisioning systems handle each new subscriber separately. The RFC then covers the addition and deletion of identifiers, the carrier-of-record versus transit distinction, the multiplicity that results in a given identifier residing in multiple destination groups at any given time, modification of the SED associated with an identifier, a change of carrier-of-record role, and the possible outcomes when an SSP indicates it is the carrier-of-record for an identifier previously associated with a different one.

Miscellaneous. Number portability is the case where a set of public identifiers is no longer associated with the original SSP but has been ported to a recipient SSP, which provides access to these identifiers via a switch on the Signaling System Number 7 network identified by the RN. Data recipient offer and accept covers the case where a peer must first accept its role as a data recipient before a peering change takes effect, or where auto-accept is configured for it. Open numbering plans cover countries where an open numbering plan is used, so that the carrier-of-record is only aware of a portion of the E.164 number, that is the TN prefix, and may not know the complete number or the number of digits; the rest of the digits are handled offline, for example by a Private Branch Exchange. An SSP can therefore be the carrier-of-record for '+123456789' and for every possible expansion of that number, such as '+12345678901' and '+123456789012', without knowing what those expansions are.
sections.plainLanguage: The use cases are the situations a protocol would have to handle: adding a subscriber's number now, adding thousands overnight, peering with another provider, sharing routing data in one of three ways, and changing who is responsible for a number. They are grouped into seven categories.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.content:
Section 4 extracts the requirements from the use cases. The objective is to make it easier for protocol designers to understand the underlying requirements and to reference and list the requirements that they support or do not. The requirements listed here are expected to be supported unless explicitly indicated otherwise, and protocol proposals are expected to indicate their compliance and to highlight the ones they do not meet. The requirements are not meant to be limiting: implementations and deployments may choose to support additional requirements based on use cases that are not listed in this document.

The seven families are these. Provisioning mechanisms: REQ-PROV-1 real-time provisioning, REQ-PROV-2 non-real-time bulk provisioning, which is optional, and REQ-PROV-3 multi-request provisioning. Interconnect schemes: REQ-INTERCONNECT-1 inter-SSP peering, REQ-INTERCONNECT-2 direct and indirect peering, REQ-INTERCONNECT-3 intra-SSP SED, REQ-INTERCONNECT-4 selective peering and REQ-INTERCONNECT-5 provisioning of a delegated hierarchy. SED exchange and discovery: REQ-SED-1 SED containing unified LUF and LRF content, REQ-SED-2 SED containing LUF-only data using domain names, REQ-SED-3 SED containing LUF-only data using administrative domains, and REQ-SED-4 support for all the other SED requirements concurrently for the same public identifier, TN range or RN. SED record content: REQ-SED-RECORD-1 the ability to provision SED record content, and REQ-SED-RECORD-2, optional, the communication of an associated TTL for a SED record.

Data management: REQ-DATA-MGMT-1 separation of responsibility for provisioning the points of ingress and other SED from the responsibility of provisioning public identifiers, REQ-DATA-MGMT-2 the ability to aggregate a set of public identifiers as destination groups, and REQ-DATA-MGMT-3 the ability to create the aggregation termed route group. Public identifiers, TN ranges and RNs: REQ-PI-TNR-RN-1 provisioning of, and modifications to, destination groups and route groups, REQ-PI-TNR-RN-2 the ability to distinguish an SSP as either the carrier-of-record provider or the transit provider, REQ-PI-TNR-RN-3 a given public identifier, TN range or RN residing in multiple destination groups at the same time, REQ-PI-TNR-RN-4 modification by moving a public identifier, TN range or RN to a different destination group via an atomic operation, REQ-PI-TNR-RN-5 the ability to indicate a change of role from carrier-of-record provider to transit or the other way, and REQ-PI-TNR-RN-6 support for modification of authority with the conditions described in UC PI #6. Miscellaneous: REQ-MISC-1 number portability support, REQ-MISC-2 the ability for an SSP to be offered a peering relationship and to accept, explicitly or implicitly, or reject such an offer, and REQ-MISC-3 support for open numbering plans.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC turns the use cases into 26 numbered requirements in seven groups, so that a protocol designer can say which ones their protocol meets and which it does not.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Session establishment data allows for the routing of SIP sessions within, and between, SIP Service Providers. Access to this data can compromise the routing of sessions and expose a SIP Service Provider to attacks such as service hijacking and denial of service. The data can be compromised by vulnerable functional components and interfaces identified within the use cases.

A provisioning framework or protocol that implements the described use cases must therefore provide data confidentiality and message integrity, and must specify mechanisms to authenticate and authorize any entity that provisions data into the registry, that is, to check that the entity is who it says it is and is allowed to use the provisioning interface. The determination of whether such an entity is authorized to provision specific data elements, such as a certain public identifier or TN range, is required, but may be left to local policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The data this protocol moves decides where calls are sent, so anyone who can read or change it can hijack or block calls. A protocol must keep it confidential and unaltered, and must check who is allowed to write.

items.title: Provisioning mechanisms
items.text: 3 requirements: real-time, bulk, and multi-request provisioning.

items.title: Interconnect schemes
items.text: 5 requirements: inter-SSP, direct and indirect peering, intra-SSP, selective peering, delegated hierarchy.

items.title: SED exchange and discovery
items.text: 4 requirements: unified LUF and LRF, domain names, administrative domains, and all of them at once.

items.title: SED record content
items.text: 2 requirements: provisioning the record content, and an optional time-to-live.

items.title: Data management
items.text: 3 requirements: separated provisioning responsibility, destination groups and route groups.

items.title: Public identifiers, TN ranges and RNs
items.text: 6 requirements: provisioning and modification, carrier role, multiplicity, atomic moves and authority.

items.title: Miscellaneous
items.text: 3 requirements: number portability, peering offers and open numbering plans.
